disease_info: Bipolar II Disorder is characterized by a recurrent course of major depressive episodes and hypomanic episodes, with no history of full manic episodes. Hypomanic episodes involve a distinct period of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy or activity that is observable by others but not severely impairing or requiring hospitalization, while depressive episodes tend to be more functionally debilitating and often drive help‑seeking. The disorder typically emerges in late adolescence or early adulthood but can first be diagnosed later in life when patterns of mood fluctuation become clearer or are triggered by significant stressors or medical changes. It is distinguished from unipolar depression by the presence of hypomania, and from Bipolar I Disorder by the absence of full mania and psychotic features, though it can still be associated with marked distress, suicidality, and impaired quality of life.

narrative.personality: Sabine is a meticulous, intellectually curious elder who combines competitive, data‑driven rigor with a deep artistic sensibility and commitment to mentoring others.
narrative.stressor: In the past year, Sabine underwent a series of health setbacks, including a minor stroke and progressive mobility issues that forced her to step back from the hands‑on STEM outreach and exhibition curation that had defined her identity for decades. The abrupt reduction in her community engagement, coupled with increasing dependence on her spouse and others for transportation and daily tasks, left her feeling as though her sharp mind was trapped in a failing body, challenging her lifelong sense of competence and usefulness. Initially she tried to compensate by throwing herself into late‑night data analysis for old projects and obsessively planning new curricula she could no longer realistically implement, but as weeks passed, the contrast between her ambitions and her physical limitations deepened her despair and rumination about aging and legacy. After two months of increasingly bleak thoughts about whether her life’s work still mattered and whether it was worth continuing, her spouse and a former mentee persuaded her to see a psychiatrist when she began voicing persistent preoccupations with death and questioning why she should keep going.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I find myself thinking a lot about death and wondering if it would be easier if I just weren’t here anymore.”

narrative.personality: Carmen is a diligent, community‑minded team player who channels her competitiveness into steady career advancement while trying to keep her life organized and financially stable.
narrative.stressor: Over the past several months, Carmen took on extra responsibilities at her busy clinic while simultaneously enrolling in courses toward her Certified Medical Manager credential, believing that pushing hard now would open doors to a supervisory role. As staffing shortages worsened, she began staying late to cover shifts, lead workflow improvement projects, and tutor newer MAs, all while studying at night and trying not to fall behind on bills after her divorce. The sustained pressure and lack of real downtime gradually eroded her usual balance; at times she would run on adrenaline, moving quickly from task to task and signing up for new projects, only to swing into periods where she felt slowed down and struggled to keep pace at work and in class. After about two months of noticeable changes in her usual rhythm—alternating stretches of overdrive and periods where coworkers commented she seemed unusually slowed and withdrawn—her clinic supervisor suggested she see a mental health professional, which Carmen agreed to after becoming worried by how markedly her energy and activity levels were fluctuating.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My body and movements feel really off lately—some days I’m racing around like I’m on fast‑forward and other days I can barely get myself moving.”

narrative.personality: Chavez is a conscientious, community‑oriented perfectionist who prides himself on disciplined leadership and tends to overextend himself out of a strong sense of duty.
narrative.stressor: Chavez’s company announced an aggressive new sales initiative with the possibility of promotion to district manager, a role he had quietly aspired to for years, placing heavy expectations on him to turn his already busy store into a top performer. In response, he began redesigning schedules, launching elaborate merchandising plans, volunteering for every regional task force, and adding extra church and community projects on evenings and weekends, convinced that demonstrating tireless effort was the only way to secure his future. Over several weeks, his days became increasingly packed from early‑morning inventory checks to late‑night planning sessions at his kitchen table, leaving little room for rest or time with his family, even as he felt driven to keep adding new goals and commitments. After about two months of this relentless pace—during which his wife and church colleagues noticed he seemed constantly keyed up and unable to slow down, followed by stretches when he would crash and struggle to sustain his usual focus—his pastor and spouse encouraged him to seek psychiatric evaluation, concerned that his pattern of escalating activity and subsequent downturns was no longer just ordinary work stress.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I can’t stop going—there’s always one more thing I have to do, and it’s starting to wear me down.”
